write.desc: The first theorems proved from the completeness axiom (the Archimedean property, density of the rationals and irrationals, existence of square and n-th roots, the nested interval property and the uncountability of the reals); they belong together because each is a short existence proof that produces a number as a supremum, or uses completeness directly, and then checks that it has the required property.

points.name: The Archimedean property
points.what: Prove that the natural numbers are not bounded above in the reals, by assuming they are, taking alpha = sup N and getting a contradiction from alpha - 1 < n for some n. Understand that this needs completeness and is not just an ordered field fact.
outside: definition of supremum as the least upper bound

points.name: Archimedean property in epsilon form: 1/n < epsilon
points.what: Derive that for every epsilon > 0 there is n in N with 1/n < epsilon, use it to prove inf {1/n : n in N} = 0, and use it as the everyday tool for choosing N in epsilon arguments.
outside: definition of infimum and its epsilon characterisation

points.name: The integer part of a real number
points.what: Prove that for every real x there is a unique integer m with m <= x < m + 1 (the floor of x), using the Archimedean property and the well-ordering of the natural numbers.
outside: well-ordering principle of the natural numbers

points.name: Density of the rationals
points.what: Prove that between any two reals a < b there is a rational m/n: pick n with 1/n < b - a, then the least integer m with m > na. Explain what 'dense' means and why the step size 1/n must be smaller than the gap.

points.name: The irrationality of sqrt 2
points.what: Prove that no rational number squares to 2, by the lowest-terms parity argument, and so see concretely that the rationals have a gap where sqrt 2 should be.
outside: parity of integers: if n^2 is even then n is even

points.name: Existence of sqrt 2 as a supremum
points.what: Prove that alpha = sup {x > 0 : x^2 < 2} exists and satisfies alpha^2 = 2, by ruling out alpha^2 < 2 and alpha^2 > 2 with a well-chosen alpha +/- 1/n. Recognise this as the model existence proof: produce a number as a supremum, then show it has the property.
outside: definition of supremum as the least upper bound

points.name: Existence of n-th roots
points.what: Adapt the sqrt 2 proof to show that every positive real a has a unique positive n-th root, using an estimate of (x + h)^n - x^n for small h.

points.name: Density of the irrationals
points.what: Prove that between any two reals there is an irrational number, for example by finding a rational q between a/sqrt 2 and b/sqrt 2 (or between a - sqrt 2 and b - sqrt 2) and checking that q sqrt 2 (or q + sqrt 2) is irrational.

points.name: The nested interval property
points.what: Prove that a decreasing sequence of closed bounded intervals I_1 contains I_2 contains ... has a nonempty intersection, by showing that x = sup of the left endpoints lies in every interval because every right endpoint is an upper bound for the left endpoints.
outside: definition of supremum as the least upper bound

points.name: Shrinking nested intervals meet in exactly one point
points.what: Prove that if, in addition, the lengths b_n - a_n can be made smaller than any epsilon > 0, the intersection is a single point, and see this as the basis of bisection arguments.
outside: lemma: if |a - b| < epsilon for every epsilon > 0 then a = b

points.name: Where nested intervals fail: open intervals and the rationals
points.what: Show that the open intervals (0, 1/n) are nested with empty intersection, and that nested closed intervals with rational endpoints closing in on sqrt 2 have empty intersection in Q, so both closedness and completeness are needed.

points.name: The reals are uncountable (nested interval proof)
points.what: Prove that no list x_1, x_2, ... contains every real number: choose closed intervals I_1 contains I_2 contains ... with x_n not in I_n, and show the point in their intersection is missing from the list.
outside: definition of countable set (a bijection with N, or a list)

points.name: Decimal expansions of real numbers
points.what: Understand that every x in [0, 1] has a decimal expansion with digits found from integer parts of 10^n x, that every decimal string defines a real as the supremum of its truncations, and that the only real numbers with two expansions are those like 0.4999... = 0.5.
outside: definition of supremum as the least upper bound

points.name: The reals are uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument)
points.what: Prove that (0, 1) is uncountable by building, from any list of decimal expansions, a decimal that differs from the n-th one in the n-th digit, choosing digits that avoid 0 and 9 so the double expansions like 0.4999... = 0.5 cannot spoil the argument.
outside: definition of countable set (a bijection with N, or a list)
Cantor's diagonal argument for decimals in outline

points.name: The irrationals are uncountable
points.what: Conclude that the irrationals are uncountable because the rationals are countable and a union of two countable sets is countable, so 'most' real numbers are irrational even though both sets are dense.
outside: a union of two countable sets is countable

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed., Springer)
where.detail: Section 1.4 Consequences of Completeness (nested intervals, Archimedean property, density of Q, existence of sqrt 2); Sections 1.5 Cardinality and 1.6 Cantor's Theorem (uncountability, diagonal argument)

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis (4th ed., Wiley)
where.detail: Section 2.4 Applications of the Supremum Property (Archimedean property, sqrt 2, density); Section 2.5 Intervals (nested intervals, uncountability, binary and decimal representations)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed., McGraw-Hill)
where.detail: Chapter 1: Theorem 1.20 (Archimedean property and density of Q), Theorem 1.21 (n-th roots)
